Package com.stzteam.features.robotlocalization.vio.sim

Class SimulatedQuestNav

java.lang.Object
com.stzteam.features.robotlocalization.vio.sim.SimulatedQuestNav
All Implemented Interfaces:
AutoCloseable
public class SimulatedQuestNav extends Object implements AutoCloseable
A Meta Quest running QuestNav, simulated.

It publishes to NetworkTables exactly what a real headset publishes, so production robot code --- the code that uses gg.questnav.questnav.QuestNav --- works unchanged and without hardware. It is the counterpart of SimulatedLimelight: there we stand in for the camera, here we stand in for the headset.

Usage


 public class Robot extends TimedRobot {
     private final SimulatedQuestNav quest =
             new SimulatedQuestNav(
                     new Transform3d(0, -0.332, 0, new Rotation3d(0, 0, Math.toRadians(-90))),
                     new QuestNavSimConfig());

     @Override
     public void simulationPeriodic() {
         quest.periodic(drivetrain.getSimulatedPose());
     }
 }
The Transform3d is the same ROBOT_TO_QUEST you pass to your real subsystem.

What makes it different from a simulated camera

  • It always reports something. A Limelight either sees the tag or it does not; a Quest always gives a pose, just with error. That is why the real content lives in VioErrorModel and not in the geometry.
  • Several frames per cycle. The headset runs at 100 Hz and the robot at 50, so each periodic() publishes ~2 frames with timestamps 10 ms apart, interpolating the pose in between. That is what makes getAllUnreadPoseFrames() return what it would really return.
  • An origin of its own. The Quest does not report field poses until the robot code calls setPose(). See QuestOriginFrame.

Mind dataTimestamp()

By default publication happens on the same NetworkTables instance the robot code consumes, and in that case PoseFrame.dataTimestamp() is useless: it is a constant 1 microsecond. That is not a bug in this class but in the topology --- that value comes from the serverTime the NT server assigns on receipt, and ntcore marks everything published locally with the sentinel serverTime = 1.

If your robot code fuses on timestamps, which is the normal case for a pose estimator, switch on QuestNavSimConfig.withNetworkClient(boolean): the simulation then publishes as an NT4 client against the robot's server, just like the real headset, and the timestamps come out correct. Everything else --- pose, tracking, battery, commands --- works the same in both modes.

On a real robot

The constructor detects RobotBase.isReal() and creates nothing. periodic(Pose2d) is an immediate return.

    • periodic

      public void periodic(edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d simulatedRobotPose)
      The headset's cycle, with a 3D pose.

      Which pose to pass, and which not to

      It has to be the truth: the pose from your physics simulation, or pure wheel odometry. Not the one coming out of your pose estimator.

      This is not a style preference. The physics feeds the sensor and the sensor feeds the estimator; feeding the sensor the estimator's output closes a loop that does not exist on a real robot. And it has a concrete symptom: a vision-corrected estimator jumps every cycle, and those jumps enter the error model as accelerations of thousands of m/s2. The impact detector mistakes them for collisions, the Quest loses tracking non-stop, and each re-acquisition adds its offset until the pose wanders off the field.

      The model filters isolated jumps with a median, but against periodic feedback no causal filter will do. If you cannot give it a clean pose, switch the automatic detection off with QuestNavSimConfig.withImpactTrackingLoss(boolean) and inject the losses by hand.

      Parameters:
      simulatedRobotPose - the robot's current simulated pose, with no vision corrections.

    • isPublishing

      public boolean isPublishing()
      Says whether the simulation is delivering data to the robot.

      In local mode it is always true. When publishing as a network client, it is false until the connection to the robot's NT4 server is established: if it stays false, the robot is not bringing its server up and not a single frame is going to arrive.

      Returns:
      true if the transport is ready.
